text: Across Chicago, by the Cook Center's count, between 75 and 95 percent of the homes sold to Black families in the 1950s and 60s were sold this way, at an average markup of 84 percent over what a white buyer paid for a comparable house.
People fought back.
In 1968, North Lawndale residents formed the Contract Buyers League.
A World War II veteran named Clyde Ross helped lead it.
More than 500 families went on a payment strike, holding their money out of the sellers' hands until the contracts were renegotiated, and more than 450 of them eventually won new terms.
But the fight was house by house, and the larger machine kept running.
Researchers at Duke University's Samuel DuBois Cook Center on Social Equity, working with the University of Illinois at Chicago, later put a number on the total damage.
Contract selling stripped between 3 and 4 billion dollars from Black Chicago.
That was money that should have become equity, a paid-off house, a down payment for a grandchild, something handed down.
Instead it flowed to the sellers, and for the families it simply vanished.
You can still measure the hole it left, decades on.
In 2022, the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances found that the median white family in America held about 285,000 dollars in wealth.
The median Black family held about 45,000.
That's a gap of more than six to one.
And here's the part that surprises people.
Black family wealth actually rose faster over those years, up 61 percent from 2019, against 31 percent for white families.
The dollar gap still widened, because Black wealth was growing off a much smaller base.
That's what makes a wealth gap so stubborn.
You can run faster and still fall further behind.
A gap that wide doesn't come from one bad decade or one set of choices.
It gets built one stripped contract, one denied loan, one priced-out block at a time, and then it gets passed down, the way wealth is, in reverse.
The family that lost a contract house in 1962 didn't just lose a house.
It lost the thing that house would have become, the inheritance, the cushion, the down payment for the next generation.
